content: Chagas disease, also referred to as American trypanosomiasis, is an illness caused by a parasite. This parasite is found in the feces of triatomine bugs, commonly known as kissing bugs. These bugs often defecate while biting humans. Infection typically occurs when individuals unknowingly rub the bug's feces into the bite wound while scratching or when the feces come into contact with the eyes or mouth. In some cases, localized swelling may develop around the bite site. However, the majority of infected individuals remain asymptomatic but carry the parasite for life. Approximately one-third of those infected will develop severe complications later in life, such as cardiac or gastrointestinal disorders, regardless of whether they experienced initial symptoms. Chagas disease is primarily transmitted by triatomine bugs in regions of Mexico, Central America, and South America, particularly in rural areas. Most travelers to these regions are at low risk of contracting the disease. However, individuals who sleep outdoors or in poorly constructed housing are at a higher risk of being bitten by these bugs. Currently, there is no vaccine or medication available to prevent Chagas disease. Travelers can reduce their risk by taking the following precautions: 1. Avoid Bug Bites: Stay and sleep in rooms that are screened or air-conditioned. Avoid sleeping in thatch, mud, or adobe housing in areas where triatomine bugs are present. Use insecticides in and around such homes. Use insecticide-treated bed nets for additional protection. Wear long-sleeved shirts, long pants, and hats to cover exposed skin. Apply EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD), or 2-undecanone. Always follow the product instructions and reapply as directed. If using sunscreen, apply sunscreen first and then the insect repellent. 2. Special Considerations for Children: Do not use products containing OLE or PMD on children under 3 years old. Avoid applying insect repellent to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, cuts, or irritated skin. Adults should spray insect repellent onto their hands before applying it to a child’s face. 3. Use Permethrin-Treated Clothing and Gear: Wear clothing and use gear (e.g., boots, pants, socks, tents) treated with permethrin. Pre-treated items can be purchased, or you can treat them yourself by following the product instructions carefully. Permethrin-treated clothing remains effective after multiple washes; check the product information for details on the duration of protection. Do not apply permethrin directly to the skin.
